topic: Basic Knowledge of Laws — Civil, Criminal & Labour

items.title: Concept of Law, its Sources, and Civil vs Criminal Law
items.body:
## What is law and where does it come from?

**Law** is a body of enforceable rules laid down by the State to regulate conduct and secure justice. In India its **sources**, in order of authority, are:

- **The Constitution** — the supreme/fundamental law; every other law is valid only if consistent with it.
- **Legislation (statutes)** — enacted by Parliament and State Legislatures; the principal modern source.
- **Judicial precedent** — under **Article 141**, law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts (doctrine of *stare decisis*).
- **Custom** — long-established usage, valid only if reasonable, certain and not opposed to statute or public policy.

## Civil law vs Criminal law

| Feature | Civil law | Criminal law |
|---|---|---|
| Nature of wrong | Private wrong (against an individual) | Public wrong (against society/State) |
| Parties | Plaintiff v. Defendant | State v. Accused |
| Object | Remedy/compensation | Punishment & deterrence |
| Standard of proof | Preponderance of probabilities | Beyond reasonable doubt |
| Outcome | Damages, injunction, specific relief | Imprisonment, fine, community service |
| Governing (substantive) law | Contract Act, Transfer of Property Act, etc. | Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 |
| Procedure | Code of Civil Procedure 1908 | Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 |

## Substantive vs procedural law

- **Substantive law** *defines* rights, duties and offences and prescribes punishments — e.g. BNS, Contract Act.
- **Procedural (adjective) law** provides the *machinery* to enforce those rights — e.g. CPC, BNSS, and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (evidence).
keyPoints: The Constitution is the supreme source of law; Article 141 makes Supreme Court decisions binding precedent.
Four main sources: Constitution, legislation, precedent, custom (custom valid only if reasonable and not against statute).
Civil law: private wrong, plaintiff v. defendant, proof on preponderance of probabilities, remedy = compensation/injunction.
Criminal law: public wrong, State v. accused, proof beyond reasonable doubt, outcome = punishment.
Substantive law defines rights/offences (BNS, Contract Act); procedural law enforces them (CPC, BNSS, BSA).
items.source: Constitution of India (Art 141); standard jurisprudence; BNS/BNSS/BSA 2023

items.title: Hierarchy and Jurisdiction of Civil and Criminal Courts
items.body:
India has a **single integrated judiciary** with the Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts for each State/group of States, and a pyramid of subordinate courts below (Articles 233–237 govern district judiciary).

## Civil side

- **Supreme Court** → **High Court** → **District Judge** (highest civil court in a district) → **Sub-ordinate/Senior Division Civil Judge** → **Munsif / Junior Civil Judge** (lowest, small-value suits).
- **Small Causes Courts** handle petty money suits summarily.
- Jurisdiction is decided by **pecuniary** value, **territorial** limits and **subject-matter**.

## Criminal side (classes of criminal courts under BNSS)

- **Supreme Court** → **High Court** → **Sessions Court** (Sessions Judge / Additional / Assistant) → **Chief Judicial Magistrate** → **Judicial Magistrate First Class** → **Judicial Magistrate Second Class**.
- **Executive Magistrates** perform administrative/preventive functions (bonds, curfew, dispersal of unlawful assembly) — not trials.
- A Sessions Court can pass any sentence including **death**, but a death sentence needs **High Court confirmation**.

## Note

The **same officer** usually presides as **District Judge** (civil) and **Sessions Judge** (criminal). Appeals move upward: district courts → High Court → Supreme Court.
keyPoints: India has one integrated judiciary: Supreme Court → High Courts → subordinate courts (Art 233–237).
Civil hierarchy: District Judge → Sub-Judge (Senior Division) → Munsif/Junior Civil Judge; Small Causes Courts for petty suits.
Criminal hierarchy: Sessions Court → Chief Judicial Magistrate → Judicial Magistrate First Class → Second Class.
Executive Magistrates handle preventive/administrative matters, not trials.
A Sessions Court's death sentence requires High Court confirmation; civil jurisdiction turns on pecuniary/territorial/subject-matter limits.
items.source: Constitution Articles 233–237; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023, Chapter II; Civil Courts Acts

items.title: Civil Procedure Basics — Suit, Decree, Order and Appeal (CPC 1908)
items.body:
The **Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC)** is procedural law governing the conduct of civil suits.

## Life of a civil suit

1. **Institution** — a suit begins with the presentation of a **plaint** (Order VII) by the plaintiff; the defendant files a **written statement**.
2. **Trial** — framing of issues, evidence, arguments.
3. **Judgment and decree** — the court pronounces judgment and draws up a **decree**.

## Decree vs Order

| Feature | Decree [Sec 2(2)] | Order [Sec 2(14)] |
|---|---|---|
| Arises from | A suit (plaint) | An application/petition |
| Determination | Conclusively determines rights on matters in controversy | May or may not conclusively determine rights |
| Classification | May be **preliminary** or **final** | No preliminary/final classification |
| Appeal | Generally appealable (Sec 96) | Appealable only if expressly listed (Sec 104 / Order 43) |

## Appeals

- **First appeal** — from an original decree, on facts and law (**Sec 96**).
- **Second appeal** — to the High Court only on a **substantial question of law** (**Sec 100**).
- **Appeal from orders** — only for the specific orders the Code allows.
- **Review, reference and revision** are other correctional remedies.
keyPoints: CPC 1908 is procedural law; a civil suit is instituted by a plaint (Order VII) and answered by a written statement.
Decree [Sec 2(2)] conclusively determines rights, arises from a suit, may be preliminary or final, and is generally appealable.
Order [Sec 2(14)] arises from an application, may not decide rights conclusively, and is appealable only if the Code allows.
First appeal from a decree lies under Sec 96; second appeal to the High Court under Sec 100 only on a substantial question of law.
Other remedies: review, reference and revision.
items.source: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Sections 2(2), 2(14), 96, 100, 104; Orders VII and XLIII

items.title: The 2023 Criminal-Law Overhaul — BNS, BNSS and BSA
items.body:
From **1 July 2024**, three new laws replaced the colonial-era criminal codes:

| New law (2023) | Replaced | Sections |
|---|---|---|
| **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** | Indian Penal Code 1860 | 358 (IPC had 511) |
| **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)** | Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 | 531 (CrPC had 484) |
| **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)** | Indian Evidence Act 1872 | 170 (IEA had 167) |

## Key changes — BNS (substantive)

- **Community service** introduced as punishment for certain petty offences (a first in India).
- New/consolidated offences: **organised crime** (Sec 111), **terrorism** (Sec 113), **mob lynching**, **snatching** (Sec 304), and **Sec 69** (sexual intercourse by deceitful means/false promise of marriage).
- **Sedition (IPC 124A) repealed**, recast as **Sec 152** (acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India).

## Key changes — BNSS (procedural)

- **Zero FIR** (register at any police station regardless of jurisdiction) and **e-FIR**.
- **Mandatory forensic investigation** for offences punishable with ≥7 years' imprisonment.
- **Time-bound justice** — e.g. judgment within **45 days** of completion of trial; charges framed within 60 days.
- **Trial in absentia** for proclaimed absconders; **videography** of search and seizure.

## Key changes — BSA (evidence)

- **Electronic and digital records** (emails, messages, server logs, device data) recognised as admissible **documentary/primary evidence**.
- Retains safeguards such as inadmissibility of confessions made to the police.
keyPoints: BNS, BNSS and BSA (all 2023) came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing IPC 1860, CrPC 1973 and Indian Evidence Act 1872.
BNS has 358 sections; introduces community service, defines organised crime (111) and terrorism (113), adds mob lynching and snatching.
Sedition (IPC 124A) is repealed and recast as BNS Section 152 (acts endangering sovereignty/unity/integrity).
BNSS (531 sections) brings Zero FIR, e-FIR, mandatory forensics for offences ≥7 years, and judgment within 45 days of trial completion.
BSA (170 sections) gives electronic/digital records the status of admissible documentary evidence.
items.mnemonic: N-S-A: Nyaya = offences, Nagarik Suraksha = procedure, Sakshya = evidence.
items.source: Ministry of Home Affairs; BNS/BNSS/BSA 2023 (in force 1 July 2024)

items.title: FIR, Cognizable Offences, Bail and the Nirbhaya Act
items.body:
## FIR and classes of offences

A **First Information Report (FIR)** is the information recorded by police about the commission of a **cognizable offence** (Sec 173, BNSS).

| | Cognizable | Non-cognizable |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | Murder, rape, theft, kidnapping | Defamation, simple hurt, public nuisance |
| Arrest without warrant | Permitted | Not permitted |
| Investigation | Police may investigate without magistrate's order | Requires magistrate's order |

## Bail

- **Bailable offence** — bail is a **matter of right** (Sec 478, BNSS); may be granted by police or court.
- **Non-bailable offence** — bail is at the **court's discretion** (Sec 480), weighing gravity, evidence and flight risk.
- **Anticipatory bail** — **pre-arrest** protection granted by the **Sessions Court or High Court** (Sec 482).

## Nirbhaya Act — Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013

Enacted after the **December 2012 Delhi gang-rape**, on the **Justice J.S. Verma Committee** recommendations:

- Widened the definition of rape; created offences of **acid attack (326A/B), voyeurism, stalking and sexual harassment**.
- Enhanced punishment, including **death** for repeat offenders or where the assault causes death/persistent vegetative state.
- The **Nirbhaya Fund** (2013) finances women's safety schemes. A 2018 amendment added the death penalty for rape of a girl below 12.
keyPoints: An FIR (Sec 173 BNSS) is registered for cognizable offences; for non-cognizable offences police need a magistrate's order.
Cognizable = arrest without warrant and investigation without magistrate's order (murder, rape, theft); non-cognizable = neither.
Bailable offence: bail is a right (Sec 478); non-bailable: bail is discretionary (Sec 480); anticipatory bail is pre-arrest (Sec 482).
Nirbhaya Act = Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013, on Justice Verma Committee recommendations after the Dec 2012 Delhi case.
It created acid-attack, stalking, voyeurism and sexual-harassment offences and enhanced rape punishment; Nirbhaya Fund set up in 2013.
items.source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (Sec 173, 478, 480, 482); Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013

items.title: Labour Law — the Four Codes, Welfare Legislation, Cyber & Consumer Law
items.body:
## Concept of social-welfare legislation

**Social-welfare (labour) legislation** protects workers — the weaker party in the employer–worker relationship — by guaranteeing minimum wages, safe conditions, social security and the right to organise, reflecting the **Directive Principles** (Art 39, 41, 42, 43).

## Why new labour laws?

Over **40 fragmented central Acts** created overlapping definitions and compliance burdens, and did not cover new forms of work (**gig, platform, contract**). To simplify and modernise, Parliament consolidated **29 central labour laws** into **four Labour Codes**, brought into force on **21 November 2025**.

| Code | Subsumes (examples) | Thrust |
|---|---|---|
| **Code on Wages 2019** | Minimum Wages, Payment of Wages, Bonus, Equal Remuneration | Universal minimum wage & national floor wage |
| **Industrial Relations Code 2020** | Trade Unions, Standing Orders, Industrial Disputes | Fixed-term employment; higher threshold (300 workers) for retrenchment/standing orders |
| **Code on Social Security 2020** | EPF, ESI, Maternity Benefit, Gratuity | Extends cover to **gig & platform** and unorganised workers |
| **OSH Code 2020** | Factories, Mines, Contract Labour, Inter-State Migrant | Single registration, licence & return; safety standards |

## Key welfare Acts (many now subsumed)

- **Minimum Wages Act 1948**, **Factories Act 1948** (health/safety/welfare), **Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act 1986** (amended 2016 — bars children below 14), **ESI Act 1948** (medical/sickness/maternity benefit), **EPF & MP Act 1952** (provident fund & pension).

## Cyber and consumer law

- **Information Technology Act 2000** (amended 2008): legal recognition of electronic records/signatures and cyber offences (hacking, identity theft, cyber terrorism Sec 66F). **Jurisdiction is difficult** in cybercrime because offences are borderless; Sec 75 asserts **extra-territorial** application.
- **Consumer Protection Act 2019** (replaced 1986 Act): consumer rights, **Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA)**, e-commerce rules, product liability, and a three-tier District/State/National Commission structure.
keyPoints: Social-welfare legislation protects the weaker worker and gives effect to Directive Principles (Art 39, 41, 42, 43).
Four Labour Codes consolidate 29 central labour laws and came into force on 21 November 2025.
Codes: Wages 2019, Industrial Relations 2020, Social Security 2020, OSH 2020; Social Security Code covers gig/platform workers.
Key welfare Acts: Minimum Wages 1948, Factories 1948, Child Labour 1986 (amended 2016), ESI 1948, EPF 1952.
IT Act 2000 governs cyber offences (jurisdiction is hard as crime is borderless; Sec 75 extra-territorial); Consumer Protection Act 2019 created the CCPA and product liability.
items.source: Ministry of Labour & Employment (four Labour Codes, in force 21 Nov 2025); IT Act 2000; Consumer Protection Act 2019
